faq.q: Why do we have two eyes instead of one?
faq.a: Two eyes give two slightly different views, which the brain combines to judge depth and distance. They also give a wider field of view and a spare if one is injured.
asks: What is the point of two eyes?

faq.a: Depth perception is the ability to see the world in three dimensions and judge how far away things are. The brain uses the difference between the two eyes' views plus clues like size and overlap.

faq.q: Can people with one eye judge distance?
faq.a: Yes, quite well. The brain uses one-eye clues: near things look bigger, cover farther things, and move faster across your view when you move your head. Only very close fine judgements are harder.
asks: Can you see depth with one eye?
How do people with one eye judge distance?

faq.a: A 3D film shows two slightly different pictures at once, and the glasses let each eye see only one of them. Your brain compares the two views just as it does in real life and feels depth.
asks: Why do 3D glasses make things pop out?
How do 3D movies trick the eyes?

faq.q: Why does my finger jump when I close one eye then the other?
faq.a: Each eye looks at your finger from a different position, so the finger lines up with a different part of the background. That shift is exactly what the brain uses to judge distance.
asks: Why does my thumb move when I blink each eye?

facts: Human eyes are on average a little over 6 centimetres apart.
The difference between the images in the two eyes is called binocular disparity.

quiz.say: You close one eye and try to touch two pencil tips together. Why is it harder?
quiz.show: Why is touching pencil tips harder with one eye shut?

options.show: The brain loses the second view it compares for depth
options.say: The brain loses the second view it compares for depth

options.show: The open eye goes out of focus
options.say: The open eye goes out of focus

quiz.why: With one eye shut there is no second view to compare, so close-up distance judgements become much harder.

wrong.0: One eye still sees colour perfectly well.
wrong.2: The open eye still focuses normally; it is depth, not sharpness, that suffers.
